The last five posts were all body topics, so I am staying in that proven area with a fresh, relatable psychology-and-body subject almost everyone has felt: hating your own recorded voice. It should drive shares and comments. Reel format, since reels carry nearly all non-follower reach. I kept it to 5 short slides and used lofi music, which was on the top performer. Since 100% of reach comes from non-followers anyway, this is a low-risk first Trial Reel test. Palette 4 continues the rotation. The caption ends with an opinion question to test comment pull.
topic: Why your recorded voice sounds strange: bone conduction, stapedius reflex, self-voice bias
hook: Why your voice sounds weird on recordings

slides.title: Two paths to your ear
slides.body: When you speak, sound reaches your inner ear through the air and through the bones of your skull.
slides.image_prompt: Anatomical skull model on a dark table with soft glowing sound waves passing through the bone toward the ear area

slides.title: Bones add the bass
slides.body: Your skull carries low tones well, so in your head your voice sounds deeper and fuller than it really is.
slides.image_prompt: Close-up of a large bass speaker cone vibrating, dust jumping on its surface, deep moody lighting

slides.title: Microphones skip the bones
slides.body: A recording only captures sound through the air. That thinner, higher voice is what everyone else hears.
slides.image_prompt: Vintage studio microphone in a dim room with thin bright sound waves drifting through the air around it

slides.title: Your ears turn it down
slides.body: A tiny middle-ear muscle tightens as you speak, muffling your own voice so it doesn't deafen you.
slides.image_prompt: Detailed anatomical ear model with a tiny glowing muscle inside the middle ear, soft blue lighting

slides.title: You actually like it
slides.body: In a 2013 study, people rated their own voice as more attractive when they didn't recognize it as theirs.
slides.image_prompt: Old cassette tape recorder on a wooden desk, a small golden heart shape resting beside it, warm light

cta: Follow so you never miss the next one
caption:
That cringe when you hear yourself on a voice note is real, and it has a physical cause. In your head, your voice also travels through your skull bones, which boost the low tones. A microphone only picks up the air, so the recording sounds higher and thinner than the voice you know.

The twist: in a 2013 study, people rated their own voice as more attractive when they didn't realize it was theirs. So the problem is mostly surprise.

Be honest: do you still hate hearing your own voice on recordings?
